question: What are the key compliance deadlines for merchant bankers under the January 2026 SEBI amendment?
ground_truth: The SEBI circular (January 2, 2026) on Merchant Bankers Regulations amendments has the following deadlines: (1) By February 2, 2026 — disclose non-SEBI regulated activities on website. (2) By April 3, 2026 — ensure compliance officer independence, close outsourced core merchant banking activities. (3) By July 3, 2026 — segregate non-SEBI regulated activities into separate business units with Chinese Wall, submit compliance report for non-SEBI regulated activities. (4) By January 2, 2027 — submit CA certified net worth certificate for categorization, ensure NISM certifications for employees, ensure principal officer has 5 years experience. (5) By January 2, 2028 — comply with underwriting obligations not exceeding 20 times liquid net worth. (6) First assessment from April 1, 2029 — minimum revenue generation requirements (Rs. 25 crore for Category I, Rs. 5 crore for Category II cumulative over three preceding financial years).

question: Can an insurer raise health insurance premiums for senior citizens by 15% in a single year?
ground_truth: No. Per IRDAI circular IRDAIV/HLT/CIR/MISC/27/1/2025 dated January 30, 2025, insurers shall not revise the premium for senior citizens by more than 10% per annum. If the proposed increase exceeds 10%, the insurer must undertake prior consultation with IRDAI. The circular applies to all Non-Life and Stand-Alone Health Insurers (except AIC and ECGC) with immediate effect. Additionally, insurers must consult IRDAI before withdrawing individual health insurance products offered to senior citizens.

question: As a Tier 4 Urban Cooperative Bank, can we provide working capital loans secured by gold to a jewellery manufacturer?
ground_truth: Yes, with conditions. Under the RBI's amended Lending Against Gold and Silver Collateral Directions (1st Amendment, September 29, 2025, circular RBI/2025-26/84), Scheduled Commercial Banks and Tier 3 or 4 UCBs may extend need-based working capital finance to borrowers using gold or silver as raw material or input in manufacturing or industrial processing. However, borrowers must not acquire or hold gold for investment or speculative purposes. Separately, lenders shall not grant advances for the purchase of gold in any form (primary gold, ornaments, jewellery, coins, ETFs, Mutual Funds) or against primary gold/silver or financial assets backed by primary gold/silver.

question: How quickly must an insurance company report a cyber incident to IRDAI, and what log retention period is required?
ground_truth: Per IRDAI circular IRDAI/GA&HR/CIR/MISC/49/03/2025 dated March 24, 2025, on Cyber Incident or Crisis Preparedness: (1) Cyber incidents must be reported to IRDAI in prescribed format within 6 hours of noticing or being brought to notice about such incidents. (2) All ICT infrastructure and application logs must be maintained and monitored for a rolling period of 180 days. Additionally, system clocks must be synchronized with NTP Servers of NIC or NPL, entities must implement a Cyber Crisis Management Plan (CCMP), and forensic auditors must be empanelled in advance with no conflict of interest (vendors handling SOC, attack surface monitoring, Red teaming, or annual assurance audit cannot serve as forensic auditors).

question: What specific changes were made to the NCS Master Circular for green debt security reviewer appointments?
ground_truth: Per SEBI circular dated February 27, 2026 (ref: HO/17/11/24(1)2026-DDHS-POD1/I/5967/2026), Chapter IX Paragraph 1.8 of the NCS Master Circular was deleted and a new Paragraph 5 was inserted. The changes align the requirements for appointing an independent third-party reviewer/certifier for green debt securities with those for social and sustainability bonds. The reviewer must be independent of the issuer and have expertise in ESG debt securities. The scope of the review and details of the reviewer must be disclosed in the offer document. The circular applies to issuers of green debt securities, recognized stock exchanges, recognized depositories, registered merchant bankers, registered debenture trustees, registered credit rating agencies, and registered ESG ratings providers.

question: We are a gold jewellery manufacturing NBFC-factor. Can we pledge our gold raw material inventory with a scheduled commercial bank to get working capital finance?
ground_truth: Yes, with conditions. Under the RBI's amended Lending Against Gold and Silver Collateral Directions (1st Amendment, September 29, 2025, circular RBI/2025-26/84), Scheduled Commercial Banks and Tier 3 or 4 UCBs may extend need-based working capital finance to borrowers using gold or silver as raw material or input in manufacturing or industrial processing. The key restriction is that the borrower must not acquire or hold gold for investment or speculative purposes — the gold must genuinely be used as input in manufacturing. Note that the bank cannot grant advances for the purchase of gold in any form (primary gold, ornaments, jewellery, coins, ETFs, Mutual Funds) or against primary gold/silver or financial assets backed by primary gold/silver. So the financing must be for working capital needs, not for purchasing the gold inventory itself.

question: As an NBFC, do we need to screen our customers against the UN sanctions list? What specific obligations apply to us under the latest RBI circular on UAPA compliance?
ground_truth: Yes. Per RBI circular RBI/2025-26/94 (DOR.AML.REC.58/14.06.001/2025-26) dated October 24, 2025, all Regulated Entities — which includes NBFCs — must comply with Section 51A of the UAPA Act, 1967. Specific obligations: (1) Ensure no accounts are held for individuals/entities on the UNSC's 1267/1989 ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List. (2) Follow the procedure laid down in the UAPA Order dated February 02, 2021, as amended on April 22, 2024. (3) Forward any de-listing requests electronically to Joint Secretary (CTCR), MHA. Requests can also be submitted to the UN Ombudsperson. The circular updates one entry in the sanctions list. Non-compliance could result in severe legal and reputational consequences due to association with terrorist financing.

question: Our company received a GST demand order covering the period July 2017 to March 2021 and we filed an appeal. Under the recent CGST Rules amendment, can we withdraw the appeal only for the 2017-2020 portion and continue fighting the 2020-2021 portion?
ground_truth: Yes. Per GST Notification 11/2025 (Central Tax, dated March 27, 2025), the amendment to Rule 164 of the CGST Rules, 2017 allows partial withdrawal of appeals related to Section 128A. The taxpayer can inform the appellate authority that they wish to pursue the appeal only for the non-specified period (i.e., April 2020 to March 2021 in this case). The appeal will be treated as withdrawn for the specified period from 1st July 2017 to 31st March 2020 or part thereof. Important caveat: no refund will be allowed for tax, interest, or penalty already paid before the implementation of these rules. This streamlines the appeal process by allowing companies to avail the Section 128A waiver for the specified period while continuing to contest other periods.

question: Our listed NBFC wants to issue green bonds to fund renewable energy projects. What does SEBI require regarding the appointment of an independent reviewer for our green debt issuance?
ground_truth: Per SEBI circular dated February 27, 2026 (ref: HO/17/11/24(1)2026-DDHS-POD1/I/5967/2026), issuers of green debt securities must: (1) Appoint an independent third-party reviewer/certifier to ascertain compliance with the definition of green debt securities and review/certify processes. The reviewer must be independent of the issuer and have expertise in ESG debt securities. (2) Specify the scope of the review by the independent third-party reviewer in the offer document. (3) Adequately disclose details regarding the independent third-party reviewer in the offer document. These requirements took effect immediately. The changes were made by deleting Chapter IX Paragraph 1.8 of the NCS Master Circular and inserting a new Paragraph 5, aligning green debt security reviewer requirements with those already in place for social and sustainability bonds.

question: We are an NBFC hiring a merchant banker for our upcoming public issue of NCDs. The merchant banker's group entity holds a 3% stake in our company. Are there any new SEBI disclosure requirements that apply?
ground_truth: Yes. Per SEBI circular dated January 2, 2026 on the Amendment of SEBI (Merchant Bankers) Regulations, 1992, merchant bankers must now disclose their involvement in marketing of issues where their holding exceeds specified limits. This disclosure is required in both the offer document and marketing material. This obligation applies to all public issues filed on or after January 3, 2026, under Regulation 21C of the MB Regulations. Additionally, the merchant banker must comply with several other new requirements including: ensuring compliance officer independence (by April 3, 2026), segregating non-SEBI regulated activities into separate business units with Chinese Wall (by July 3, 2026), and meeting revised capital adequacy requirements on a phased basis.

question: Can our NBFC reduce the interest rate spread for an existing corporate borrower before 3 years to prevent them from refinancing with a competitor bank?
ground_truth: Yes, with conditions. Per RBI circular RBI/2025-26/83 (DOR.CRE.REC.51/13.03.00/2025-26) dated September 29, 2025, amending the Interest Rate on Advances Directions 2016: Banks may reduce other spread components for a loan category earlier than three years for customer retention on justifiable grounds. However, this must be done (1) in a non-discriminatory manner, and (2) in terms of the bank's policy. The circular applies to Banks and Regulated Entities (REs) offering floating interest rate on EMI-based personal loans. Additionally, the amendment allows REs to provide borrowers the option to switch to a fixed rate at the time of reset of interest rates — the RE's policy may specify the number of times a borrower can switch during the loan tenor.

question: Our company has a floating rate term loan from an NBFC. At the next interest rate reset, can we request to switch to a fixed rate instead? What are the rules around this?
ground_truth: Yes, this option may be available. Per RBI circular RBI/2025-26/83 dated September 29, 2025, amending the Interest Rate on Advances Directions and the August 18, 2023 circular on Reset of Floating Interest Rate on EMI-based Personal Loans: Regulated Entities (including NBFCs) may provide borrowers the option to switch to a fixed rate at the time of reset of interest rates. The RE's policy may specify the number of times a borrower can switch during the loan tenor. This modifies Paragraph 2(ii) of the August 2023 circular and related FAQs (FAQ No. 3(b), FAQ Nos. 4 and 5). Note: Whether this option is available depends on the specific NBFC's policy — the circular enables but does not mandate REs to offer this switch option.

question: Our listed NBFC wants to raise funds by issuing green NCDs to finance our renewable energy lending portfolio. At the same time, we're losing corporate borrowers to competitor banks and want to reduce interest rate spreads to retain them. What are the regulatory requirements we need to satisfy across SEBI and RBI?
ground_truth: This involves obligations under both SEBI and RBI: **SEBI (Green Debt Securities):** Per SEBI circular dated February 27, 2026 (ref: HO/17/11/24(1)2026-DDHS-POD1/I/5967/2026), the NBFC must: (1) Appoint an independent third-party reviewer/certifier who is independent of the issuer and has expertise in ESG debt securities. (2) Specify the scope of the review in the offer document. (3) Adequately disclose reviewer details in the offer document. If engaging a merchant banker for the NCD issue, the MB must also comply with the January 2, 2026 amendment requirements — including disclosing involvement in marketing of issues where their holding exceeds specified limits (Regulation 21C, applicable to issues filed after January 3, 2026). **RBI (Interest Rate on Advances):** Per RBI circular RBI/2025-26/83 dated September 29, 2025, the NBFC may reduce other spread components for a loan category earlier than three years for customer retention on justifiable grounds. This must be done in a non-discriminatory manner and in terms of the NBFC's policy. Additionally, the NBFC may offer borrowers the option to switch to a fixed rate at the time of interest rate reset.

question: We are a listed gold jewellery manufacturer. We have working capital loans secured by our gold inventory from SBI, a pending GST appeal for demand orders covering 2018-2020, and we're planning to issue green NCDs to fund our transition to recycled gold sourcing. What are the compliance requirements we need to track across RBI, GST, and SEBI?
ground_truth: This spans three regulators: **RBI (Gold Collateral):** Per RBI circular RBI/2025-26/84 dated September 29, 2025 (1st Amendment to Lending Against Gold and Silver Collateral Directions), the company's working capital finance secured by gold inventory is permitted — SCBs may extend need-based working capital finance to borrowers using gold as raw material in manufacturing. However, the company must not acquire or hold gold for investment or speculative purposes. The bank cannot grant advances for the purchase of gold in any form (primary gold, ornaments, jewellery, coins, ETFs, Mutual Funds). **GST (Appeal Withdrawal):** Per GST Notification 11/2025 dated March 27, 2025, the company can partially withdraw its appeal for the specified period (July 2017 to March 2020) under the amended Rule 164 of CGST Rules, 2017 related to Section 128A, while continuing to contest any remaining period. No refund will be allowed for tax, interest, or penalty already paid before the rules took effect. **SEBI (Green NCDs):** Per SEBI circular dated February 27, 2026, the company must appoint an independent third-party reviewer/certifier with ESG debt securities expertise, disclose the scope of review and reviewer details in the offer document. This aligns with the revised Chapter IX Paragraph 5 of the NCS Master Circular.

question: Our mid-sized company has floating rate loans from three different banks approaching reset dates, and our HR team is getting complaints from senior employees about steep health insurance premium increases from our group insurer. Are there any recent regulatory changes that help us on both fronts?
ground_truth: Yes, recent circulars address both concerns: **RBI (Floating Rate Reset):** Per RBI circular RBI/2025-26/83 dated September 29, 2025, amending the Interest Rate on Advances Directions: (1) At the time of interest rate reset, the company may request to switch from floating to fixed rate — Regulated Entities may now offer this option, and their policy may specify how many times a borrower can switch during the loan tenor. (2) The company can also negotiate for early spread reduction — banks may reduce other spread components earlier than three years for customer retention on justifiable grounds, provided it's non-discriminatory and per bank policy. **IRDAI (Senior Citizens Health Insurance):** Per IRDAI circular IRDAI/HLT/CIR/MISC/27/1/2025 dated January 30, 2025: Insurers shall not revise the premium for senior citizens by more than 10% per annum. If the increase exceeds 10%, the insurer must undertake prior consultation with IRDAI. Insurers also cannot withdraw individual health insurance products offered to senior citizens without IRDAI consultation. This applies to all Non-Life and Stand-Alone Health Insurers (except AIC and ECGC). The company can point its insurer to this circular if the proposed increase exceeds the 10% cap.

question: Our NBFC is preparing a public NCD issue through a Category I merchant banker, and we just received the latest RBI circular updating the UNSC sanctions list. Our compliance officer wants to know: what are all the overlapping obligations we need to handle right now from both SEBI and RBI?
ground_truth: The NBFC faces concurrent obligations under both regulators: **SEBI (Merchant Banker Regulations):** Per SEBI circular dated January 2, 2026 on the Amendment of SEBI (Merchant Bankers) Regulations, 1992: (1) The merchant banker must disclose involvement in marketing of issues where their holding exceeds specified limits — required in both the offer document and marketing material (Regulation 21C, applicable to issues filed after January 3, 2026). (2) The MB must have an independent compliance officer (by April 3, 2026). (3) The MB must have closed any outsourced core merchant banking activities (by April 3, 2026). (4) The MB must have NISM Series-IX and Series-IIIA certifications for employees (by January 2, 2027 for existing employees). (5) The MB must segregate non-SEBI regulated activities into separate business units with Chinese Wall (by July 3, 2026). The NBFC should verify its MB meets these requirements before proceeding. **RBI (UAPA Sanctions):** Per RBI circular RBI/2025-26/94 dated October 24, 2025: (1) The NBFC must ensure no accounts are held for individuals/entities on the updated UNSC 1267/1989 ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List. (2) Follow the UAPA Order dated February 2, 2021 (amended April 22, 2024) procedures. (3) Forward any de-listing requests to Joint Secretary (CTCR), MHA. The sanctions screening should be run against the updated list immediately, including screening NCD subscribers as part of KYC/AML compliance.
